work_packages.name: A program plays sounds into a buffer with no device, placed, pitched, looped and limited, and a test reads exactly what would be heard
work_packages.quality_bar: A mixer as dependable as a shipped game's: a crowded moment degrades by dropping its quietest sounds, and never by crackling, clicking or stalling a frame. Correctness held as `SIM-2D` holds it: one script, one digest, the same on every target. No reference game is named, because no item here is judged by ear or by eye: how it sounds is the owner's to judge, in `GAME-SDK` WP19.

items.statement: The mix, rendered to a buffer with no device at 48 kHz stereo, from sounds the test makes by integer arithmetic. Build this item first: the others rest on it. (1) With nothing playing, every frame is zero. (2) One play of a mono sound at volume 1 and pitch 1 with no place gives the sound's samples, each divided by 32,768, in both channels, bit for bit, from the first frame of the next pull, and zeros after its last frame. This holds for a sound one frame long, one shorter than a pull and one longer than four pulls, and the voice is free after the last frame. (3) A stereo sound with no place gives its first channel in channel 0 and its second in channel 1. (4) Two plays of one sound 480 frames apart give the sum of the two, so the second does not cut the first. (5) A volume `v` gives each sample times `v`. (6) Pitch 2 gives every second source sample exactly and lasts half as long. Pitch 0.5 gives each source sample at every second frame and lasts twice as long. (7) At each of pitch 0.9, 1.07 and 1.1, a sound 4,800 frames long whose samples rise by one 16-bit step a frame lasts 4,800 divided by the pitch frames, to within one frame, and its frame `k` is the source's value at position `k` times the pitch, to within two 16-bit steps, for every frame more than two source samples from either end. (8) A volume above 1 or below 0, and a pitch above 2 or below 0.5, are clamped to the nearest of those and counted as clamped. A volume or pitch that is not finite drops the play, which is counted as a bad value. (9) The reference script, with each command applied at its frame, gives the same frames bit for bit when pulled 1, 37, 128, 512 and 4,096 frames at a time and in a rotation of those sizes. (10) The reference script's digest equals the digest kept beside the crate's tests. Guard: CPU tests on the buffer, in `./dev check`.

A place and the listener, in the buffer. (1) A mono sound placed at the listener's position is centred and has the power of the same sound played with no place. (2) With the place straight ahead at 0, 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4 of its radius, the gain is `(1 - d/radius)²` of the gain at the listener. At the radius and at twice the radius the play is dropped and counted as out of range, which the record keeps apart from every fault. (3) A place on the listener's left, against its right vector, is louder in channel 0, and one on its right is louder in channel 1. At one distance, the summed power of the two channels is the same at five pans from hard left to hard right. (4) A stereo sound with a place is summed to mono before it is panned. (5) Turning the listener's right vector about swaps the two channels' levels. (6) A place moved, in steps between pulls, along a line through the listener's position: the pan passes through the centre, and no frame's gain in either channel differs from the frame before by more than one glide step. (7) The listener moved and turned between pulls while a long sound plays: the gains reach the new values, and no frame's gain moves by more than one glide step. (8) A place or a listener that is not finite is dropped and counted as a bad value, and the listener stays where it was. Each comparison is at the tolerance its test states. Guard: CPU tests on the buffer, in `./dev check`.

The limit and the pool, in the buffer. In (1) to (5) the sound is mono with every sample the same value `s`, small enough that forty voices of it sum below the clip's knee, and each play has no place, volume 1 and pitch 1, so a frame in which `k` voices of the sound are mixed holds exactly `k × s / 32,768` in both channels. Forty plays, numbered 1 to 40, are applied at frames 0, 1,200, 2,400 and so on to 46,800. A play that starts when applied at frame `f` covers the frames from `f` to `f` plus the sound's length less one. In each of the five cases: the plays that start are the ones named, read from each play's outcome; every other play has the fate `limit`; the record's counts of plays started and of plays dropped by the limit are those numbers; and every frame, from frame 0 to 1,200 frames past the last voice's end, holds `s / 32,768` times the number of started plays that cover it. So what is rendered is the sum of every play that started, and not a count kept beside one voice. (1) A limit of 4 and a sound 48,000 frames long: plays 1 to 4 start and plays 5 to 40 are dropped. A forty-first play, applied at frame 48,000, when the first voice has rendered its last frame, starts. The frames hold one copy from frame 0, two from 1,200, three from 2,400, and four from frame 3,600 to frame 49,199. (2) A limit of 4 and a sound 14,400 frames long: plays 1 to 4, 13 to 16, 25 to 28 and 37 to 40 start, and the other twenty-four are dropped. The frames hold four copies from frame 3,600 to frame 57,599. (3) A limit of 4 and a sound 480 frames long: all forty start. The frames hold one copy for 480 frames from each play's frame, and zeros between. (4) A limit of 1 and a sound 14,400 frames long: plays 1, 13, 25 and 37 start, and the other thirty-six are dropped. The frames hold one copy from frame 0 to frame 57,599, and never two. (5) No limit, a sound 48,000 frames long and a pool with room for forty: all forty start, and the frames hold forty copies from frame 46,800 to frame 47,999. (6) A limit on one sound does not count another sound's voices: with four voices of one sound sounding, a play of a second sound with a limit of 4 starts. (7) With the pool's share for sounds that happen full, a new play that would be louder than the quietest voice there takes its place: the displaced voice reaches silence by a ramp with no step larger than one ramp step, and is counted as displaced. A new play that would not be louder is dropped, with the fate `pool`. (8) A sound that happens never displaces an emitter's voice, and an emitter never takes a voice from the other share. Guard: CPU tests on the buffer, in `./dev check`.

Emitters, in the buffer, judged by the one policy of the design's mechanism 5: eligible, loudness, the margin, the pass in its three steps, and the earlier-started emitter ranking as the louder of two equals. (1) An emitter's voice wraps from its sound's last frame to its first with no gap and no repeated frame, over at least three wraps: the frames are the sound's samples in order, times the gain. This holds for a sound one frame long, one shorter than a pull and one longer than a pull. (2) Setting its volume, setting its pitch and moving it each change the gains or the speed by a glide, and leave its position in the sound where it was. (3) Holding it takes it to silence by a ramp and freezes its position, and letting it go ramps it back from the frame it was held at. Ending it ramps it out and frees its voice. (4) Of emitters with places, only those inside their radius are eligible. With room in the emitters' share, one that comes inside its radius holds a voice after the next update and one that leaves has given it up after the next update, and neither makes a step in the output larger than one glide step. An emitter with no place is eligible wherever the listener is. (5) With one voice in the emitters' share, a margin `m`, and two eligible emitters, of which A holds the voice at loudness `L`. While B's loudness is `L × (1 + m/2)`, A keeps the voice over 100 updates. When B's loudness is raised to `L × (1 + 2m)`, B holds the voice after the next update and A's voice ramps out. When B's loudness then falls to `L × (1 + m/2)`, and then to `L / (1 + m/2)`, B keeps the voice over 100 updates at each. With A and B equally loud from the start, the one started first holds the voice over 100 updates. This holds with places and again with neither emitter having a place, where one of the two holds no voice. (6) With 10,000 emitters laid out from a seed, more of them eligible than the emitters' share, of which 2,000 move at each of ten updates while the listener moves: after each update the emitters holding voices are exactly those that the policy, written out plainly in the test and run on the same data from the same start, gives. Every one of them is eligible, they number the share, and no emitter without a voice is louder than one with a voice by more than the margin. (7) A sound replaced while voices play it: those voices finish on the data they started with, and a play made afterwards uses the new data. The test watches the old data's release itself, and not through the allocation counter, which does not count frees: the old data is still held after every pull while those voices sound and after 1,000 more pulls made with no call on the handle, and it is released inside a later call on the handle. Removing a sound ends its emitters. Guard: CPU tests on the buffer, in `./dev check`.

Glides, ramps, the clip and the volumes, in the buffer, read with a sound of constant value so that the output is the gain. (1) The effects volume scales sounds that happen and emitters, and the master volume scales everything. A change to either while a sound plays reaches its new value by a glide: no frame's gain moves by more than one glide step. (2) Stopping, holding, displacing and ending a voice each reach silence within the configured ramp length, in steps no larger than one ramp step. (3) A sound that happens is at its gain in its first frame, and an emitter's voice starts at zero. (4) Below the clip's knee every frame leaves the mix unchanged, bit for bit. (5) With every voice of the pool sounding a full-scale sound at volume 1, every output sample is inside -1 to 1, the output rises wherever the sum rises, and the record counts the frames that reached the knee. (6) The clip is continuous at the knee: outputs just above and just below it differ by no more than their inputs do. Guard: CPU tests on the buffer, in `./dev check`.

When pulling stops and starts, in the buffer, through the two calls a sound output uses to say so. This is C11's rule for an interruption. (1) A play called while pulling, whose command the mix has not applied when pulling stops: after pulling starts again no frame holds it, and its outcome is `interrupted`, under its event identity and its tick. (2) A voice of a sound that happens that is part-way through when pulling stops renders no frame after pulling starts again, and is counted as cut by the interruption. (3) A play called while nothing pulls is never heard, and its outcome is `nothing pulling`. (4) A play called after pulling starts again is heard from the next pull, and its outcome is `started` with the new epoch. (5) An emitter that was sounding when pulling stopped goes on from the frame of its loop it had reached. Its volume and its place, the listener and the three volumes, each changed while nothing pulled, are the latest set when it sounds again. An emitter started while nothing pulled sounds, and one ended then does not. (6) Read with an emitter whose sound has a constant value, the output's gain after pulling starts again rises from silence over one ramp, in steps no larger than one ramp step. (7) The output epoch is one higher after each stop. Across two stops, of plays called in each of the three epochs, the only ones heard are those the mix applied in the epoch they were called in. (8) A new mix made for a handle that already has sounds, emitters, volumes and a listener sounds those emitters at those values, and no play made before it existed is heard. Guard: CPU tests on the buffer, in `./dev check`.

What the mix reports, in the buffer. (1) Every play call returns a play number at once. Over a script of plays that crosses one stop and start of pulling, the numbers are 1 for the first call and one more for each call after it, whatever the play's fate. (2) For a script of plays, each with its own event identity and tick, that meets each of the eight fates at least once, started, `limit`, `pool`, `out of range`, `nothing pulling`, `interrupted`, `queue full` and `bad value`: the outcomes read back hold exactly one for each play, found by its play number in whatever order the outcomes are listed, with that play's event identity, its tick, the epoch it was called in and the fate the script expects. (3) Two plays made for one event, with the same event identity and tick in the same epoch and with different volumes, in three cases. With room in the command queue for only one of the two: one outcome is `started` and the other is `queue full`, each under the number its call returned, and the number with `started` is that of the play whose volume the rendered frames hold. With one of the two placed outside its radius: that play's number has `out of range` and the other's has `started`. With room and range for both: both sound, and each number has `started`. (4) When more outcomes are produced between two reads than the list holds, the count of outcomes lost is the excess, and the record's other counts are what they are without the loss. (5) With the command queue full, a play is dropped with the fate `queue full`, and a change to an emitter, a volume or the listener made while it was full is applied once there is room, as its latest value. No call waits. (6) For a scripted case that makes each of these happen a known number of times, the record gives exactly that number: voices sounding and the most there have been, emitters, how many are eligible and how many hold a voice, plays started, plays that never started under each of the seven other fates, voices displaced, voices cut by an interruption, outcomes lost, values clamped, frames that reached the knee, the queue's high-water mark, frames pulled and the output epoch. (7) Adding a sound with no frames, one with a channel count other than 1 or 2, and one more sound than the mix was made for each return a typed error that names the cause and leave the mix as it was. Guard: CPU tests on the buffer, in `./dev check`.

A pull allocates nothing, and a frame's calls allocate nothing once a scene is set up. (1) Over the reference script and one interruption, counted on the pulling thread after the mix is made, no pull allocates or reallocates, including the pulls in which voices start, end, are displaced and are ramped, in which commands are applied, and in which a new output epoch begins. (2) Counted on the calling thread after the script's sounds are added and its emitters started, the handle's play, set, move, hold, listener, volume, update and read-the-outcomes calls allocate nothing. The test kit's counter counts allocations and reallocations and does not count frees, so that a pull frees nothing is WP1.4(7)'s to show and WP1.10's to read. Guard: CPU tests with the test kit's counting allocator, in `./dev check`. C11 asks this of an audio callback.

The mix builds as a WebAssembly module that imports nothing. One documented command builds it for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and the built module's import list is empty. Run under Node, that module renders the reference script, with each command applied at its frame, to the digest kept beside the crate's tests, pulled 128 frames at a time and again 512 at a time. Node stands in for Chrome's engine here, and WP4 runs the module inside Chrome's audio worklet. Record: the module's build and its digest under Node. The build command is kept, because a web game's build step calls it.

The mix's cost is recorded, with the machine's load at the time. (1) The time to render one minute of the fullest case, every voice of the pool sounding a placed sound at a pitch other than 1 while its gains glide, natively and in the mix module under Node, each as a share of real time. (2) The time of one update of the handle with 10,000 emitters, of which 2,000 moved and the listener moved. (3) The default sizes of the pool, of its two shares, of the command queue, of the list of outcomes and of the table of sounds, each with its reason. (4) The starting values of the ramp length, the glide step, the clip's knee, `near` and the emitters' margin. The check fails only on a missing measurement, or where a render in (1) takes longer than the sound it renders. Record: tripwire rows taken under load, kept in the working folder.
The mix is one piece of code that nothing can make wait, it gives the same bits on every target, and it holds nothing of a game's and makes no choice that is a game's.
items.ask: Read `thrum-audio` and its tests. 1. Is there one implementation of mixing: do the buffer, the mix module and whatever a sound output will pull all compile the same source for voices, gains, the pool and the clip, with no second path behind a `cfg`? 2. Follow a pull from its entry to its return. Does anything it executes take a lock, wait on anything, allocate or free, read a file or a clock, or call the operating system? Look at a replaced sound's data in particular: can its last holder be the mix, so that a pull would free it? 3. Does any call on the handle take a lock a pull could hold, or wait for a pull? 4. Does the mix path use only operations whose results are fixed on every target: is there a platform maths function, a fused multiply-add, or a table built with one? 5. Is every gain change a glide or a ramp counted in frames, with none worked out once a pull? 6. Does the crate hold any world state, name any game type, or depend on a renderer, a window or a shell? Does it ever choose between two plays, refuse one or order one by its event identity or its tick? 7. Are the crate and each outside dependency registered in `.config/architecture.toml` with an exact version, and is every licence permissive?

findings.name: An emitter restored on resume can keep sounding after it ends
Releasing a restored emitter can leave it held
findings.different: The prior hold during entry now fades correctly. Here the post-resume release command is discarded and the selected loop stays silent.

findings.name: An emitter volume changed while the queue is full can be lost on resume
findings.different: The earlier master mute now reaches the mix during continuous plays. This emitter change reaches the queue once, is rejected at the restored snapshot revision and is never retried.

work_packages.name: A .wav or .ogg is cooked into a sound or a music track, and music plays from its compressed form, loops from its loop point and cross-fades
work_packages.quality_bar: A cook as strict as the engine's other product kinds: a bad source is named and refused, and a bad product never reaches a frame. Music as a shipped game plays it: it starts at once, loops without a seam and changes without a hole. The decoder is held to the codec's specification, bit for bit against its reference. No reference game is named, because no item here is judged by ear or by eye: how it sounds is the owner's to judge, in `GAME-SDK` WP19.

items.statement: The cook turns a source into a sound product: 16-bit samples at 48 kHz with the source's channel count. (1) A 48 kHz 16-bit `.wav`, mono and stereo, cooks to exactly its own samples. (2) A 1 kHz tone as a `.wav` at 22,050, 44,100 and 96,000 Hz, as an 8-bit, a 24-bit and a 32-bit float `.wav` at 48,000 Hz, and as an `.ogg` at 44,100 and 48,000 Hz, each mono and stereo, cooks to a 1 kHz tone. Its length is the source's to within one frame at 48 kHz for a `.wav`, and to within the tolerance the test states for an `.ogg`. Its zero crossings over its length are a 1 kHz tone's to within 1%, and its level is the source's to within 1 dB. (3) Resampling is band-limited. An 8 kHz tone in a `.wav` at 22,050 Hz cooks to an 8 kHz tone at the source's level to within 1 dB, and the level of what it holds at 14,050 Hz is at least 40 dB below that tone's. A 30 kHz tone in a `.wav` at 96,000 Hz cooks to a sound whose level is at least 40 dB below the source tone's. (4) A stereo source with a tone in one channel only keeps it in that channel. (5) Each of these is refused with a message that names the file and the cause, and makes no product: three channels; no frames; a `.wav` in an encoding other than integer or float PCM; a `.wav` cut short; an `.ogg` cut short; an `.ogg` that holds a stream other than Vorbis; a file that is neither, whatever its extension. Guard: CPU tests on sources of a second or less, in `./dev check`.

A sound product and a music product are validated when opened, before any frame is exposed. (1) Each of these is refused with a named error and no panic: another kind's marker; a product cut short, at every length from nothing to one byte less than whole; a frame count the payload does not hold; a channel count other than 1 or 2; a rate other than 48,000; a codec the reader does not know; a loop point at or past the end. (2) For a seeded set of 10,000 single-byte changes to a valid product of each kind, opening either refuses the product or gives one whose every frame is read, and for music decoded, with no panic and no read outside the product. Guard: CPU tests on small products, in `./dev check`. A cooked format is where a fault is silent and costly.

The music codec is QOA as its specification defines it, checked against the reference implementation at the revision the provenance record pins. The specification fixes what a decoder gives and leaves an encoder free, so the decoder is held exactly, and the cook's encoder is held to streams that decode and to its source, and never to another encoder's choices. (1) The engine's decoder gives exactly the samples the reference decoder gives, for fixture streams the reference encoder wrote, mono and stereo, including a last frame that is not full. (2) Streams the cook's encoder writes, mono and stereo, are decoded by the reference decoder to exactly the samples the engine's decoder gives, checked against a kept digest of the reference's output. (3) A cooked track holds what its source holds, channel for channel. The source is stereo, with a 440 Hz tone in its first channel and a 1 kHz tone in its second, cooked as music from a `.wav` at 48,000 Hz and again from an `.ogg` at 44,100 Hz, and the track is decoded by the engine's decoder. The track's first channel is a 440 Hz tone and its second a 1 kHz tone: each channel's zero crossings over its length are its tone's to within 1%, and its level is its source channel's to within 1 dB. In each channel, the level of what it holds at the other channel's frequency is at least 20 dB below its own tone's. The track's length is the source's exactly for the `.wav`, and to within the tolerance the test states for the `.ogg`. A mono `.wav` holding the 440 Hz tone cooks to a one-channel track that meets the same frequency, level and length. (4) The engine's decoder allocates nothing. Guard: CPU tests on fixtures of a second or less, in `./dev check`.
items.check: cargo nextest run --locked --offline -p thrum-audio --test it -E 'test(/^codec::/)' --no-tests=fail && cargo nextest run --locked --offline -p thrum-cook --test it -E 'test(/^sound_codec::/)' --no-tests=fail

items.statement: Music in the buffer, from cooked tracks the test can tell apart in the output, so that each track's gain is read at every frame. A fade's `t` runs from 0 at the change to 1 at the end of the fade time, and gains are compared to within 0.01. (1) Saying a track from silence plays it from its first frame, with gain `sqrt(t)` over the fade time given. (2) A looping track plays to its end and goes on from its loop point: over at least three passes the frames are the decoded track's frames in exactly that order. This holds for a loop point of zero, one in the middle of the track that falls inside a codec frame, and the last frame. A track with no loop point ends, and its stream slot is then free. (3) A change from one steady track to another with a fade of one second. At `t` of 0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 and 1 the first track's gain is 1, `sqrt(3/4)`, `sqrt(1/2)`, `sqrt(1/4)` and 0, and the second's is 0, `sqrt(1/4)`, `sqrt(1/2)`, `sqrt(3/4)` and 1. From each frame to the next across the fade, the first's gain never rises and the second's never falls. After the fade only the second sounds, and the record shows one stream. (4) Saying the current track again changes nothing: its position goes on, and the record shows one stream. (5) A second change, to a third track with a new fade of one second, made part-way through the fade of (3): in one run at `t` of 1/20, and in another at `t` of 1/2. With `s` that `t`, over the new fade the first track's gain is `sqrt(1 - s) × sqrt(1 - t)`, the second's is `sqrt(s) × sqrt(1 - t)` and the third's is `sqrt(t)`, at `t` of 0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 and 1. From each frame to the next across the new fade, the first's and the second's never rise and the third's never falls. At every frame from the first change to the end of the new fade, the squares of the three tracks' gains sum to 1, to within 0.04, so the music's level is carried through both fades. The record shows three streams until the new fade ends, and one after it. (6) Two further changes, to a fourth and then a fifth track, made while those three streams sound: no new stream starts until the fade under way ends, the fifth track then fades in as `sqrt(t)` over the time it was given while the third falls as `sqrt(1 - t)`, the fourth never sounds, and the record never shows more than three streams. In another run the second of the two asks for the third track, which is the current one: nothing starts when the fade ends, and the third track plays on alone. (7) Saying no track fades the current one out as `sqrt(1 - t)` over the time given, and its stream slot is then free. Said while three streams sound, it does not wait: each of the three falls from the gain it has, times `sqrt(1 - t)`. A fade time of zero changes within one ramp. (8) The music volume and the master volume scale music and glide. The effects volume does not touch it, and holding emitters does not touch it. (9) A track given to the mix in pieces: a stream that reaches the end of what has arrived renders silence, the record counts those frames, and when the next piece arrives the stream goes on from the same frame of the track. (10) Adding a track allocates no more than its cooked bytes and a fixed amount: a track six times as long allocates more only by the difference in cooked bytes. A pull allocates nothing while three streams sound. (11) The record gives the streams sounding, the current track and its position. Guard: CPU tests on tracks of a few seconds, in `./dev check`.

Through the cooker as a game uses it, from a source folder to the store. (1) A `.wav` and an `.ogg` are published as sound products under their logical names, and resolve by name and kind through the manifest. (2) A source with the small file beside it that says it is music, with a loop point in seconds, is published as a music product whose loop point is that time at 48 kHz, to the frame. With no loop point the track does not loop. (3) Saving a changed source publishes a new generation with the new product, and saving the small file beside a sound makes it music. (4) A source the cook refuses is named with its cause in the cook's report, and the store keeps the last good product under that name. A loop point at or past the track's end is refused the same way. (5) The same source cooks to the same bytes every time. Guard: CPU tests on sources of a second or less, in `./dev check`.

The reference script gains a cooked sound played and looped, a looping track through two passes, and a cross-fade. (1) Its new digest is kept beside the crate's tests, WP1.1's test holds it natively, and the log says why it changed. (2) The mix module, built by WP1's command and still importing nothing, renders the script under Node to that digest, with the cooked products handed to it as bytes. (3) Recorded with the machine's load: the time to render one minute with the pool full and three music streams sounding, two fading out and one fading in, natively and in the module, each as a share of real time; the cooked bytes for one second of a mono and of a stereo sound and of a mono and of a stereo track; and the cook's time for one second of `.wav` and of `.ogg` source. The check fails only on a missing measurement, a digest that differs, or a render that takes longer than the sound it renders. Record: the module's digest under Node and tripwire rows taken under load, kept in the working folder.
items.check: python3 scripts/audio.py module && python3 scripts/audio.py costs

items.statement: What ships links no authoring code, and a game without sound links no sound code. (1) `thrum-audio`'s normal dependency closure, for the Mac, for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` and for the iPhone simulator, holds none of `thrum-cook`, the cook's decoders or its resampler, and no renderer, window or shell package. (2) The normal closures of `thrum-app` and of the V1 game hold no `thrum-audio`. (3) The repository guards' list of authoring packages names the cook's decoders and its resampler, so a later landing that links one into a shipping package fails `./dev check`. The check first confirms that every package it reads is in the workspace's metadata, so it cannot pass by finding nothing. Guard: the repository guards, in `./dev check`.
Everything that came from outside the repository is recorded in `docs/provenance/AUDIO.md` and is permitted.
items.ask: Read `docs/provenance/AUDIO.md` beside the files it names. 1. Does it list every file copied or translated from elsewhere and every fixture made with an outside tool, each with its source, its revision or version, its licence and the command that made it? Look for QOA's reference in particular: the fixture streams, and any translated code. 2. Is every licence it names permissive, with none GPL or share-alike? 3. Is every outside crate this work package added used by `thrum-cook` alone, and registered in `.config/architecture.toml` with an exact version? 4. Does anything hold a music track decoded: is a stream's memory the cooked bytes and a fixed amount, as the design's mechanism 8 says?
